When a concerted effort was made to unionize the WHT paper some of the staff, notably Jason Armstrong who recently showed up as a writer for Civil Beat (CB), didn't see the wisdom in doing so and destroyed any possibility of the paper's staff remaining organized against a cut throat management and ownership. As such we do not have any real paper and rely on CB for our news.

I hope the staff of the Star-Advertiser can endure. Though their union doesn't seem strong enough for the task. God Bless them!

orig_text: Rob does not mention that there are strictly speaking two types of dividends, the type that are subject to gross-up and dividend tax credit (the gross up can play havoc for people trying to avoid claw-back on their old age pensions) and the interest-type dividends paid by mortgage investment corporations (MICs) . MICs are allowed to expense their dividends, so in the hands of investors, they are fully taxable. However, there is no "gross up" like there is for dividends eligible for tax credit and the returns on investment are usually much higher (often 7 per cent or more). Of course, there is a fair amount of risk attached to MICs, so investors have to be cautious. Also, their capital gains come very slowly over time. Not for all investors, to be sure, but MICs are worth considering. (And, no, I don't work for one of them, but I have shares in a couple of them - but not Home Capital.) (Payouts by REITs are not considered to be dividends, and are in a different class of investment.)

The right of a professional to refuse a service based on religious objections is a complex issue and only growing more so. 

Obviously, conscience should be respected in situations where a person is asked to directly participate in something they find morally objectionable, like a nurse assisting in an abortion. 

But on the other end of the spectrum are things like bakers refusing to sell wedding cakes to gay couples, an act that's completely immaterial to gay marriage itself. (As I write this, the Supreme Court has just agreed to hear one such case.)

You can make a sound argument for a pharmacist refusing to sell abortifacients. But should that extend to contraceptives too? And, if so, should condoms be included? As long as we're talking about not enabling bad behavior, should merchants be allowed to refuse the sale of cigarettes and liquor to adults, even though those things are legal?

These are not easy questions and there is no one-size-fits-all answer.

Two stories, one a father who signed over a property to his son, to help him out in a tough housing market, and the son then lost a large enough portion of that through divorce that he had to sell.

That cost the single mom about twenty thousand dollars, most of it legal fees, and a re-mortgage.

Stories?  Reader here will have hundreds. 

Mostly - it's the money.

I think it was fair to read Violet's definitive assertion as pertaining to the historical Jesus, whose self-identity is sheer speculation.

As I understand it: The gospel writers, most conspicuously the author/s of John, associated Jesus with the sacrificial Passover lamb. But even before the gospels, the "Philippian Hymn," which is said to predate Paul, implicitly contrasts the disobedient Adam with Jesus the obedient son, "to the point of death, even death on a cross." The earliest Christians apparently believed the Crucifixion was God's will (otherwise "obedience" here makes no sense), a sentiment echoed in Gethsemane when Jesus says "not what I want but what you want." Why would God will the Messiah be crucified? Well, as Paul relates in another pre-Pauline formulation (1Cor 15:3-6), Christ died for our sins and was raised on the third day "according to the scriptures." (Personally I don't find this answer satisfactory.)

Jesus's Eucharistic Words suggest self-sacrifice.

A couple of years before, it was warmer, but just _above_ the threshold to make snow, even up in the mountains. I am not an environmentalist except in that I value the air we breathe and tire of seeing ugly housing developments increasingly taking over valuable green spaces. I don't really fancy myself any sort of "ist". I like to be open to new ideas, and I think the notion of pushing ever outwards has been tried and does not work particularly well if our goals are something other than gridlock and environmental degradation.

I think we do need high speed trains, but there is certainly room for much greater population intensification in Toronto prior to having suburbs explode all over the place. At its highest density Toronto (which often fancies itself the Manhattan of the North) is about 13000 people per square kilometer. This is about half that of Manhattan. (I am just using approximate figures as there are disputes about the numbers in different sources). Rather than building out, we probably need to build up.

"The average homeowner only save about $600 with the mortgage interest deduction"

Maybe nationwide across all existing mortgages and tax situations, but...

Actual savings depends on where itemizing (mortgage interest, property tax, state/local tax) puts you compared to the standard deduction and where you fall in the marginal tax rates.

If my itemized deductions are $15k, the standard deduction is $12,700, and I'm solidly within the 15% bracket, the fact that I have a mortgage only "saves" me about $345 (15% of that $2300 difference).

If, however, my itemized deductions are $30k and I'm near the 15%-to-25% tax rate threshold, the fact that I have a mortgage might save me $4,000 in federal tax.

Once you cross the threshold where itemized deductions are greater than the standard deduction, you start saving [tax bracket %] X additional interest. While the first $10k of interest might only yield the $345 savings above, the next $5k of interest might save another $750 or more in tax.

A bit of background. The apparently eye-popping fee is the result of the SECs Acquired Fund Fees requirement (implemented in 2014) which forces funds that own BDCs to report BDC's expenses as if they were their own. 
I've never quite fathomed out the SEC's rationale for this move but it had some ramifications in the early days, e.g. both Russel and S&P removed BDCs from their indices as a result.

Rgerdless, I believe that BDCs are worthy of consideration by those investors seeking primarily a robust yield and who have a moderately high risk tolerance. I've held a number for years (currently hold 9).

I would recommend, for those who are interested, investing directly in individual BDCs, not via an ETF.

Some names to consider are ARCC (current yield 9.3%), GSBD (8.0%), MAIN (7.1% - calculated taking into account the regular semi-annual supplemental dividends of $0.2750) , NMFC (9.4%). Their Investor Presentations and latest quarterly reports are a good starting point for research.

That is, the BEP's report doesn't tell us how Canadians of other ethnicities report their experience of microaggressions; nor does it tell us how Black Canadians' answers to the questions have changed over time.

So the Black Experience Project can collect some interesting qualitative data and highlight perceived problems. In particular, the interview responses can give us a glimpse of *how* racism is felt by Black people to work.

But the BEP can't give us a very clear picture of how widespread racism is, given both the lack of representativeness and the lack of any comparison between groups or over time.

I remember Vatican II, which started when I was in high school. Many of us were filled with idealism and hope. As Wordsworth said about the French Revolution, "Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive,/But to be young was very heaven!" I know what happened to the ideals of the French Revolution -- the red terror, the 18th Brumaire, and so on. The idealism of that revolution was lost; and the idealism of the late 60s was lost also. I will not speak of the political reasons for the loss of idealism: Vietnam, Kent State, Watergate; but our idealism was also in our Church.

We felt a spirit saying "Behold! I make all things new!"  I have been to a Mass concelebrated by a Catholic priest and an Episcopalian priest, and we expected reunion between Rome and Canterbury because each would recognize the other as sisters in Christ. We were foolish to think such things, but it was such a wonderful dream, and far better than the more cynical attitude I have been left with.

Fast? The Wildrose Alliance Party contested 3 elections: 2008, 2012 and 2015. The Alberta Alliance Party, the first fracturing of the right, was formed in 2002, and ran in 2004 before merging with the new Wildrose Party. Overall, the right has been fractured for a decade (at least) yet that did not prevent the PCs from majorities until 2015.

The Liberal slide does little to explain the NDP rise given the NDP rose over 30% while the Liberals fell just under 6%. Nor does the fracturing of the right really provide much explanation. Reality is, many PC voters shifted to Notley, clearly not viewing Wildrose as a rational alternative and actually the Wildrose lost vote percentage. Combined, there was a swing of about 26% away from the right (PC & Wildrose). 

Nothing in 2015 can predict 2019, but the 'fracturing of the right' thesis does not really explain past results. 2015 might be just a blip like 1990 Ontario as people try on something different, but then again, it might not.

Interesting workup.  Wrong conclusion, I think.

Craig Medred has been following a data string that suggests there are too many hatchery pinks released in the North Pacific.  They are voracious feeders that out compete other salmon species - king, silver, chum and red - for what is naturally found in the ocean.  It may explain the awful king and silver returns the last decade.  And the hatchery pinks benefit commercial fishermen.

So if this is a problem, how do you solve it?  One way would be to start raising commercial pinks via aquaculture - fish farming - in their own pens so they aren't out in the open out competing other species for available food in the wild.

Somewhere along the line, we are going to have to get a handle on precisely what the carrying capacity (total number of feeding salmon) of the North Pacific actually is.  I don't mind commfish making a living.  I do mind them destroying everyone else's access to fish in order to make that living.  Cheers -

< even though in English, depending on context, “men” can mean “males” or “humans.”>
English is a dynamic language. People who speak and write it correctly and well no longer use the masculine noun or pronoun to stand for the whole of the human species.
This is even more true in translating from the Latin, which has specific and different words to refer to the male of the species (vir = [a] man); to the female of the species (mulier = [a] woman); and to the whole of the species (hominem = person). 
It is incorrect to translate "Qui propter nos homines et propter nostram salutem" as "for us men."  If that was the intended meaning, Latin has a perfectly good word for that. It would read: "Qui propter nos viros ..." -- excluding women.  The Latin word "homines" is inclusive and should be translated inclusively. The failure to do that is poor English -- it represents (in the best case scenario) the laziness of the translators or (in the worst case) their ill-will.

I'm not arguing for thinning out the human herd and leaving non-producers at the mercy of the elements, but simply pointing out that science and faith give us very different perspectives on life, and facile statements about their compatibility are wishful thinking.

In my experience this is not a problem. On our annual trips to southern Florida we average more than 1,200 km a day: an initial drive of around 400 km, followed by a series of slightly shorter legs interspersed with charging stops ranging from 20 to 40 minutes each (total charging time on the road is around 2 hours per day). We enjoy the opportunity to get out of the car and go to a café or restaurant for a quick snack or meal while the car is charging. We have also met some interesting folks at the charging stations, and have never had to wait for a free charger. Cold weather is not a problem, I recall that it was minus 37 degrees during the northern leg of one trip. 

Unlike a gas car, many of which have notoriously unreliable and non-linear gas gauges (which have left me stranded), we have found the electric cars provide reliable information about the remaining range and, after 140,000 km of EV driving have never been stranded or suffered from “range anxiety”.

FACT #8: FLUORIDE IS THE ONLY MEDICINE ADDED TO PUBLIC WATER

Fluoride is the only chemical added to water that doesn’t actually treat the water. Chlorine, for example, is added to kill bacteria so that we can drink the water without getting sick. Fluoride, by contrast, is added to prevent a disease (tooth decay) that is not caused by drinking water.

Fluoridation proponents claim that fluoridated water is not a medication because, in their view, it’s no different than adding iodine to salt or vitamin D to milk. What proponents fail to acknowledge, however, is that iodine and vitamin D are both essential nutrients; but fluoride is not.

An essential nutrient is something the body has a physiological demand for. If we don’t have enough iodine, for example, our thyroid gland won’t function properly. Although fluoride advocates sometimes claim that fluoride is a “nutrient,” the National Academy of Sciences has repeatedly confirmed that this is not the case.[40]

Your contrasting "objective sin" with sin as a construct is confusing and not entirely correct.  

First of all, there IS "objective sin," or what St. Thomas calls "material sin."  It is not the kind of sin that brings moral guilt, and is not what most people think of when they think of sin.  

Secondly, you are right to say that sin as we usually mean it --- "actual" sin --- is subjective, in that it requires the actor's knowledge of the wrongness of the act and the intent to commit it.  Your phrasing, however, invites the conclusion that nothing is objectively wrong, which I don't think you really want to say.

Finally, to say there is "only a construct of sin" seems to say that sin does not exist except as a creation of the human mind.  But physical acts are real, and when a real act violates God's will --- which is also real --- there is nothing about the fact of violation that reduces the sin to a mere human construct.  If you disagree, pinpoint the error.

They then proceeded to require all plans to include coverage for more conditions. They said all of this would still work because of increased efficiency (something our government is so well known for) and greater bargaining power. Clearly, the doctors were going to be on the losing end of this bargain as insurance companies were required to cover more people for more things for less money, and we all know how willing insurance companies are to operate at a loss. The result has been insurance companies dropping out of the ACA market, leaving some areas with as few as one provider (i.e. a monopoly), and doctors dropping out of the market because of low reimbursement rates.

Do we get it now?

It is time to repeal and replace this mess caused by Obama and the Democrats. Support repeal and replacement of the ACA.

orig_text: There is a difference between pain and suffering, and this is part of the confusion over pain control. Pain is the actual physical sensation, and certainly can be excruciating, which is what narcotics are for. Suffering includes pain, but also includes all the emotional turmoil that surrounds it. So someone who has fibromyalgia, for example, may also experience depression because of loss of independence or inability to work, anxiety related to inability to accept the diagnosis, thinking perhaps that the pain is due to undiagnosed cancer, or frustration at friends or family who may not seem to appreciate the sufferer's distress. None of the latter can be helped by narcotics, but if the only question the health practitioner asks is "do you have pain?" the answer will always be "yes", and the danger is that the dose of pain medication will continue to be increased even although that will only add to the individual's problems rather than relieving them.

See the true result of declawing, Krista? Thousands of declawed cats are dumped in kill shelters each yr. They've lost their claws and now they lose their lives. FOR A COUCH. Sick
Get informed. Educate. Don't mutilate.
Sarah A. West, DVM,DACVR

~40% of the votes garnered 49.4% (43 seats) for the BC Liberals.
~40% of the votes garnered 47.1% (41 seats) for the NDP.
~16% of the votes garnered 3.4% (3 seats) for the Greens.

In my opinion, a move to a more proportional model can't come soon enough.

For reference, elections in BC have had multiple changes to voting processes in the last 100 years:
- Women were granted the right to vote (1917)
- Two elections in the 1950s were held with a system that did not use first past the post.
- The voting age changed in 1952 and 1992
- Advance voting days and hours have increased significantly.

All of this is to say that our system has changed regularly and one of its strengths is its capacity to continue to improve.

What is fundamental is the fact that one (adult) person gets one vote.

It is not an option to pretend that this system has been static or unchanging in the history of this province (never mind this country).

Good luck to all of us.

The nature of death in general is an important and little understood issue; I am glad you brought it up.

For every living creature, its death is a natural evil. Such death is a systemic evil too, since the life shared by all creatures cannot be sustained without the constant cycle of death. From another point of view, or another measure, as you say, the dying of older creatures is a "good" thing, leaving space and resources for younger ones. But it remains true that in itself, death is an evil.

Killing too is always an evil, even in circumstances when it is justifiable or excusable. And one of the most horrid of the systemic evils that humans must face is having to feed on the tissue of other living creatures for survival. We can at least mitigate that by feeding only on the non-sentient.

Many wisdom traditions, e.g. Christianity, teach that our own personal death is not to be feared -- and that is true too. But it does not justify imposing our beliefs on the dying of others.

The spirit of constant and total self-gift is what gives joy. 

Most people spend their entire life resisting what seems like either pablum, blather, or a paradox.

The beautiful idea of the Communion of Saints is generally barely understood by most Catholics.

The idea is that - through the Body of Christ - we are intimately & in a very real way "connected".

Your heroic sacrifice for your family in Chicago can benefit me in some real way in my home state. 

My lack of sacrifice or sincerity in facing the motives for my "un-gift" in my family can effect a priest on the other side of the world.

We are connected. My strivings, your strivings to love with the very heart of Christ can materially help priests, but not just "generic priests", but this or that priest or lay person.

So our "lack of generosity" in living family life can cause shortages of "generosity" elsewhere, including the priesthood. 

It takes faith to fully live the "Communion of Saints", but it leads to joy

Reminds me of 1966.  I'd been working in New Orleans during the summer after my freshman year at TWC, and I bought a used car, an old Mercury, from a guy from Pennsylvania that had PA tags on it.  I paid cash, he signed over the title and gave me a Bill of Sale, then I drove to El Paso.  A month or so later I registered the car in Texas and got Texas tags, but I hadn't put them on yet when I came out of class with a buddy and found a "boot" on my tire for unpaid parking tickets.  I assessed the situation, noticed a gap between the steel plate and the lug nuts, jacked up the car, removed the lug nuts, and put the tire and the boot in my trunk, and drove off on the spare, eventually putting the boot in the fraternity trophy case.

Alas, they tracked me down.  The Dean of Students wasn't amused.  Had to return the boot, pay all the tickets, and go on social probation.  I enlisted at the end of that semester and came back 3 years later, considerably matured.

"Crazy" and similar terms ("mad," "insane") as epithets for something or someone that seems far beyond the reasonable is probably as old as language itself.  The idiom can be found many times in  Greek tragedy.  I assume it's in the Bible, but I haven't specifically looked for it. It's in the Quran.  It's in Shakespeare and Milton.  In modern discourse, it's commonplace to call Hitler "insane" (which he wasn't in any clinical sense, except possibly for Parkinsonism).  

While Kennedy is right that people suffering from mental illness should not be associated with an idiom of opprobrium, the fact is that "crazy" and its synonyms have no scientific or clinical meaning.  They are popularly understood in a non-clinical sense.  While the "Political Correctness" meme is a poisonous one, it's possible to be ridiculous in our desire to sterilize ordinary language--which is, wonderfully, as various and unpredictable as people themselves are.

orig_text:
I directed Waiting for Godot as a student at York University way back in 1969. Since then I've seen many productions, in Toronto, Stratford, New York, and more.This one, by Soulpepper, is perhaps the very best. It was nuanced, moving, funny, profound, engaging, human.  A bromance in the context of the vastness of time and the ambiguity of identity and relationship. It felt letter-perfect, with a couple of remarkably fleshed-out performances. The pacing, and variety of silence and loud action is right on. Yes, Sam B. would have preferred an open set,
and I would have liked that, too. But that's a quibble, not enough to outweigh the
wonderful work by this director and these actors. I'm in no way related to any of them in any way, but as an audience member felt only rewarded by a very intelligent, well-staged, wonderfully performed classic which felt fresh, timely
and timeless.

Eighty pounds is about 50-70% of an average woman's body weight. To be honest, I would not like it if my husband gained 50-70% of his body weight.  It's not only the way he would look, but I have a hard time believing it would not affect his mood, outlook, energy levels and sex drive. That said, I hope we have enough shared history that I would be patient and supportive to help him solve the problem, but I would never deny there is a problem.

By the same token, I think this is a problem for their marriage, especially if the writer already feels like he wants a divorce. Sucking it up is not an answer. That said, the only way his wife solves this problem is with his wholehearted support. I think he needs to try that. Go to counselling, adopt a healthier lifestyle as a couple and be encouraging rather than judgmental. If she's willing to work at it, they can probably save this marriage. If she refuses, there may be no future for them.
